title: Given the root of a binary tree, return its node values grouped by level, from top to bottom and left to right within each level. Explain the Tree Breadth First Search pattern.
shortTitle: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (BFS Level by Level)

s1_definition.profdef: Tree BFS visits nodes level by level using a FIFO queue. Seed the queue with the root, then for each level record the current queue size, dequeue exactly that many nodes while enqueuing their children, and collect each level's values into its own list. Time is O(n); space is O(w) where `w` is the maximum width.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India's org chart has the branch manager at the top, then department heads, then clerks. To list staff rank by rank, you start with the manager in a waiting line, call them, add their direct reports to the back of the line, and keep processing the line one full rank at a time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use a queue, snapshot the level size, drain exactly that many nodes while enqueuing their children, one list per level.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Tree BFS visits nodes level by level using a FIFO queue. Seed the queue with the root, then for each level record the current queue size, dequeue exactly that many nodes while enqueuing their children, and collect each level's values into its own list. Time is O(n); space is O(w) where `w` is the maximum width.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India's org chart has the branch manager at the top, then department heads, then clerks. To list staff rank by rank, you start with the manager in a waiting line, call them, add their direct reports to the back of the line, and keep processing the line one full rank at a time.

**One line to remember:** Use a queue, snapshot the level size, drain exactly that many nodes while enqueuing their children, one list per level.

sections.s2_technical:
The essential trick is capturing `levelSize = queue.size()` at the start of each level before dequeuing. That snapshot tells you exactly how many nodes belong to the current level, so you drain precisely that many, enqueuing each node's non-null children, and everything enqueued during that drain belongs to the next level. This cleanly separates levels without any depth markers.

For example, using a `Queue<TreeNode> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.offer(root);` then `int size = q.size(); for (int i=0;i<size;i++){ TreeNode n=q.poll(); level.add(n.val); if(n.left!=null)q.offer(n.left); if(n.right!=null)q.offer(n.right);}` collects one level per outer iteration.

A senior-level nuance is the space profile: BFS space is bounded by the widest level, which for a balanced tree is about n/2 at the bottom, whereas DFS depth-first uses stack proportional to height. When the tree is wide and shallow, DFS may use less memory; when it is deep and narrow, BFS may. The level-size snapshot is the reusable core that every Tree BFS variant builds on.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India organizes its approval hierarchy as a binary tree of approval nodes, with the branch head at the root and sub-approvers beneath. To display an org-style approval chart rank by rank, the system must output each level of approvers as its own row. This is exactly level-order traversal: process the tree with a queue and group nodes by level.

The code contains an `ApprovalNode`, an `OrgChartService` with `levelOrder(root)`, and a demo building a small approval tree.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: tree with root 1, children 2 and 3, and leaves 4, 5 under 2 and 6 under 3.

Step 1: Queue holds [1]. levelSize=1. Drain node 1, record 1, enqueue 2 and 3. Level list is [1]. Queue is [2,3].

Step 2: levelSize=2. Drain 2 (record 2, enqueue 4,5), drain 3 (record 3, enqueue 6). Level list is [2,3]. Queue is [4,5,6].

Step 3: levelSize=3. Drain 4, 5, 6; none have children. Level list is [4,5,6]. Queue empties.

Step 4: Result is [[1],[2,3],[4,5,6]].

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Level order approval chart: [[1], [2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: tree rooted at 1
    │
    ▼
  OrgChartService.levelOrder()  (FIFO queue)
    │ size=1 drain[1]  enqueue 2,3     → [1]
    │ size=2 drain[2,3] enqueue 4,5,6  → [2,3]
    │ size=3 drain[4,5,6]              → [4,5,6]
    ▼
  Output: [[1],[2,3],[4,5,6]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Binary tree level order traversal is the foundation of the Tree Breadth First Search pattern, and it rests on a FIFO queue plus one small but essential trick: at the start of each level I snapshot the current queue size. That snapshot tells me exactly how many nodes belong to this level, so I drain precisely that many, recording their values and enqueuing their children, and because every child I enqueue during that drain belongs to the next level, the levels separate cleanly without any depth markers or sentinels.

The algorithm runs in linear time, and its memory is bounded by the widest level rather than the height, which is the opposite of depth-first traversal. I mention that trade-off because for a deep narrow tree BFS can be the lighter choice while for a wide shallow tree DFS can be, and the right answer depends on the shape.

In my work at the National Bank of India this rendered an approval org chart. The approval hierarchy was a binary tree with the branch head at the root and sub-approvers beneath, and the display needed each rank of approvers as its own row. Processing the tree with a queue and grouping nodes by the level-size snapshot produced exactly that rank-by-rank layout, and I always stress that this level-size snapshot is the reusable core that every other Tree BFS variant, from zigzag to right-view, is built on.
